title: How to Find and Hire the Best Product Managers (September 2026)
summary: Learn how to hire the right product managers for your team with expert tips on identifying top talent and improving your recruitment process. (September 2026)
body_markdown:
Knowing when and how to[hire product managers](https://www.dover.com/) is one of the harder early-stage decisions a founding team faces. Get it right and you have someone who connects customer needs to engineering priorities, owns the roadmap, and keeps the team moving toward product-market fit. Get it wrong and you either slow down because no one is driving product decisions, or you bring in the wrong archetype for where the company actually is. This guide covers the full picture: timing, sourcing, career ladders, interview signals, and what the 2026 PM market looks like for startups actively hiring.


**TLDR:**


-


Most startups hire their first PM between employee 10 and 19, or wait until 100+, depending on founder product depth.


-


AI-focused PM roles now account for 8 to 10 percent of open positions globally, with compensation roughly double traditional PM pay.


-


Clarify which PM archetype you need before writing the job description: a builder-PM or a strategic PM.


-


Assess product sense by checking if a candidate taught you something new about your own product during the interview.


-


Some tools pair a free ATS with on-demand recruiting support, letting you post to 100+ job boards and add fractional help averaging $2,000 to $7,000 per hire only when needed.


## What Is Product Management, and Why Do You Need a Product Manager?


A product manager identifies customer needs and business objectives, articulates what success looks like, and aligns cross-functional teams to ship toward product-market fit. They sit at the intersection of engineering, design, and the market, the person responsible for connecting what customers need to what the team builds.


### So What Does the Role Involve?


-


Partner with engineering to align on the roadmap, set deadlines, and manage deliverables


-


Deeply understand buyer personas and user needs


-


Monitor the market and run competitive analyses


## When Should I Hire My First Product Manager?


This table, pulled from[Lenny’s Newsletter](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/when-to-hire-your-first-product-manager) (a popular Substack created by Lenny Rachitsky, an angel investor and former PM at Airbnb) finds that **the first PM is generally hired as the 15th - 100th employee, and 2 - 4 years after founding** . From our internal data, we find that the majority of companies hire a PM at the 10-19 employee mark, or the 100+ employee mark.


Obviously, each company is different, but three factors seem to contribute to waiting longer to hire your first full-time PM:


1.


Founders with deep product sense (e.g. Shopify)


2.


Building a product that isn’t primarily user-facing (e.g. Stripe)


3.


Long early beta period (e.g. Airtable)


Once you decide the time is right, choosing the right[recruitment sources](https://www.dover.com/blog/sources-of-recruitment) is one of the first practical steps to take.

## What Is the Typical Career Ladder for a Product Manager?


### **Associate / Junior Product Manager**


Works on a specific feature or scoped area, still under the guidance of a senior PM.


### **Senior Product Manager**


Owns a product or product area end-to-end, focusing on driving outcomes and maximizing the value of existing investments.


### **VP of Product / Head of Product**


The most senior product leader sets overall strategy, manages the PM team, and represents product at the executive level. In startups, this role often carries direct budget responsibility alongside hands-on roadmap ownership.


## What’s Changing About Product Management in 2026?


The PM job market has rebounded sharply. Product coach Ant Murphy tracked roughly[42,000 open PM roles on LinkedIn](https://www.antmurphy.me/newsletter/how-product-is-changing-in-2026) in early 2026, double the count from the same period a year earlier. For startups in active hiring mode, that shift matters: the pool of available candidates is larger, but so is the competition for the best ones.


Two trends are reshaping what a strong PM hire looks like in 2026:


-


**AI PM roles are growing fast.** AI-focused product management positions account for 8 to 10 percent of all open PM roles globally, with AI PM searches up roughly 41 percent year over year. These roles command a substantial compensation premium: product coach Pawel Huryn, who tracks PM pay, puts AI-focused PM compensation at around $245,000 in the US compared to roughly $123,000 for traditional PMs.


-


**The generalist PM is harder to defend.** Companies are increasingly hiring for specialization: AI-native PMs, growth PMs, monetization PMs, and PMs with a GTM focus. For an early-stage startup hiring its first PM, the practical step is clarifying which archetype you actually need before writing the job description, a builder-PM who can work closely with engineers versus a strategic PM who owns roadmap, stakeholder alignment, and GTM coordination.


PM Archetype Best For Key Strengths Watch Out For


**Builder-PM** Early-stage teams with a small engineering org Hands-on roadmap execution, close eng collaboration, rapid iteration May struggle with stakeholder alignment at scale


**Strategic PM** Teams ready to coordinate across GTM, design, and exec stakeholders Roadmap ownership, cross-functional alignment, GTM coordination Can be slower to ship without strong execution support


None of this changes the fundamentals of what makes a strong PM hire, curiosity, execution ability, product sense. But it does raise the bar on clarity about the role before you start the search.


## What Skills and Requirements Should I Look For?


While product managers typically have engineering or product marketing backgrounds, there are a few soft skills that will require more than one interview to suss out.


That being said, at a high-level, these are the general requirements that you’ll want to scan a resume for and ask about when assessing applications and conducting preliminary phone screens:


-


Experience with product development from ideation to launch


-


Effective communication/cross-functional collaboration skills


-


Exceptional writing and editing skills combined with strong presentation and public speaking skills


-


Technical experience or basic coding knowledge, especially if they come from an non-traditional background for PMs (like consulting)


The following **“soft” skills** are key to a product manager’s success. You’ll want to ask them in the second remote screen, as well as throughout the onsite and final interview process. We’ve provided examples of strong and weak answers as well, so you can align everyone in your interview loop.


### Collaboration


A product manager will have to function as a mediator between customers, and different departments (namely engineering). They’ll need to be good at delegating, and they’ll also need to effectively compromise and argue for various improvements in the product with various stakeholders.


#### Interview questions:


-


“Tell me about a time you disagreed with an engineer on your team and how you resolved it.”


-


What aspect of product management do you find the least interesting?


### Execution


It’s not enough to have a PM with a vision. You need someone who is capable of execution, defining deadlines and goals, as well as success metrics. Execution involves other important qualities like time-management, effective communication, and excellent people management skills.


#### Interview question:


- Pick a project you’re proud of that took 3-9 months. Walk me through it from beginning to end. I’ll ask questions along the way.


### Research


A PM with genuine curiosity and a drive to do whatever customer research a decision requires will consistently outperform one who ships on intuition alone.


#### Interview question:


- Tell me about a time you did user research on a product/feature and that research had a big impact on the product.


### Product Sense


To put it simply, great product managers should love products. Especially as an early-stage company, product knowledge and interest is key in getting over the tough hurdles of finding product-market fit, iterating on product features, and getting different departments on board with roadmap prioritization.


#### Interview questions:


-


How would you improve feature X in our product?


-


Tell me about a great product you’ve encountered recently. Why do you like it?


Product sense is hard to score in real time. A useful check at the end of a call, drawn from Ken Horton’s essay “[How to Hire a Product Manager](https://www.bringthedonuts.com/essays/productmanager.html) ”: did the candidate show creativity about where your product could go, echo a concern your team already has, or teach you something new about your own product? That last one is the strongest signal; it shows they’re willing to speak critically and think beyond the brief.


### Impact


Measuring impact in previous roles is your best signal when determining the success of a PM hire. We define some things to look out for below, but generally it’s important that they’re able to express what they’ve built in the past, and how that product or feature was successful in its target market on a qualitative and quantitative basis.


#### Interview questions:


-


What’s the most important or impactful product you shipped?


-


What made it so important or impactful?


-


Would it have been as impactful without you, and why?


### Technical Knowledge


Technical fluency helps PMs translate requirements to engineers and explain complexity to non-technical stakeholders.


#### Interview questions:


-


How would you define X to a non-technical person? OR


-


How would you describe X product to a five-year-old?

## FAQs


### When should a startup hire its first product manager?


Most startups bring on their first PM between the 10th and 19th employee, though some wait until 100+. Founders with deep product backgrounds, companies building infrastructure-layer products (instead of user-facing ones), or teams in extended beta periods tend to wait longer without meaningful consequence.


### What skills and requirements should I look for in a product manager?


Look for experience with product development from ideation to launch, strong cross-functional communication, and technical fluency. Key soft skills include collaboration, execution, research ability, product sense, and measurable impact in prior roles. Product sense is best assessed by whether a candidate can teach you something new about your own product during the interview.


### Do I need a recruiter if I’m already using an ATS?


An ATS covers the infrastructure side of hiring: posting to job boards, collecting applications, and keeping candidates organized. What it doesn’t do is source passive candidates or bring market context to a role with weak inbound. For roles with steady applicant flow, an ATS alone can be sufficient. For senior or hard-to-fill positions, a fractional recruiter layered on top fills the sourcing gap, with both working from the same pipeline so the hiring team keeps full visibility.


## Final Thoughts on Hiring Product Managers for Your Startup


Knowing how to[hire product managers](https://www.dover.com/) well depends less on any single interview question and more on knowing what archetype your company actually needs at this stage, where to find candidates with genuine product sense, and having a process that keeps the search moving without monopolizing founder time. For early-stage teams without a dedicated recruiter, Dover is worth looking at: the free ATS lets you post to 100+ job boards and manage every applicant in one pipeline from day one, and if the search needs more hands-on support, fractional recruiters are available on a per-hire basis, typically averaging $2,000 to $7,000 per hire with no retainer required. The right fit for your PM search depends on your stage, your founders’ product depth, and how much capacity your team has to run the process itself.
